newsitem.title: ZIMBABWE: Britain sees investment scope in Zimbabwe.
newsitem.headline: Britain sees investment scope in Zimbabwe.

text.p: Britain said on Wednesday its investment drive into Zimbabwe has not been slowed down by a controversial privatisation deal between the southern African state and a Malaysian company.

Britain's Trade Minister Anthony Nelson told a business luncheon in Harare, his country -- whose companies currently hold the biggest foreign investment stake in Zimbabwe -- were determined to explore business opportunities in new areas such as telecommunications, information technology and power.

"Whatever controversies may have happened...we have to look ahead. I think there are plenty of opportunities for all," he said in clear reference to the Zimbabwe-Malaysia power deal signed in September amid charges by many Zimbabweans and Western countries that it appeared underhand.
It was Zimbabwe's first major privatisation deal in an unfolding programme.

Zimbabwean President Robert Mugabe has stoutly defended the pact -- under which Malaysian power producer YTL Corp Bhd would take a 51 percent stake in the privatisation of Hwange Thermal Power Station by investing Z$6 billion (U.S.$568 million) -- as above board and told Western critics "to go to hell".
"Our ambassadors were questioned by four certain Western countries," he said this week. "I told them to go to hell because Hwange thermal plant is ours and we do what we want with it."
"I would want to see more joint ventures among people in the south...let there be more outcries as we go into partnership with each other," he said to leaders from 16 Third World states.

Before the signing of the letter of intent, Zimbabwe's Electricity Supply Authority (ZESA) had invited bids and six foreign firms had been shortlisted with a British company top while YTL at the bottom of the list.

Britain's Nelson urged Zimbabwean authorities to boost their country's investment profile, saying they needed this to ensure sustained growth and to cut unemployment, currently running at about 50 percent.
"(For British companies), all we ask for is fair chance," he said. Nelson was scheduled to meet several Zimbabwean government leaders, including Mugabe, during a three-day visit ending on Thursday.
